Highway expansion is more practical than public transit in sprawling Texas cities.

anchors.title: Why doesn't Texas have better public transit?
anchors.body:
Houston, Dallas, Austin, and San Antonio are among the largest cities in the country, but they all have minimal public transit compared to similarly sized metro areas. The reasons are complex — low density, car-centric development patterns, political resistance, and funding structures that favor highways.

Why has Texas lagged so far behind on transit, and is that starting to change?

comments.body: Texas cities grew around the car. Low density and spread-out development make transit inherently harder to serve. You can't just drop a subway into a city that was built for freeways.

replies.body: But Houston's light rail exceeded ridership projections from day one. The demand is there — we just haven't built the supply. Cities don't have to stay car-dependent forever.

comments.body: The funding incentives are backwards. Federal and state money flows to highway expansion almost automatically, but transit projects have to fight for every dollar. The playing field isn't level.

anchors.title: Austin's Project Connect: Worth the investment?
anchors.body:
Austin voters approved Project Connect in 2020 — a $7.1 billion investment in light rail, bus rapid transit, and other transit improvements. It's the largest infrastructure project in Austin's history.

But costs have already risen significantly, timelines have slipped, and some question whether light rail makes sense for a city with Austin's geography and growth patterns. Was this the right investment?

comments.body: I voted for Project Connect but I'm worried about the cost overruns. We're already billions over the original estimates and construction hasn't really started on the rail components.

replies.body: Every major transit project in the country goes over budget — that's not unique to Austin. The question is whether the long-term benefit justifies the cost, and for a city growing as fast as Austin, it absolutely does.

comments.body: Austin's traffic is unbearable. I-35 is a parking lot for hours every day. We needed this investment 20 years ago. Even with cost overruns, doing nothing would cost us more in lost productivity and quality of life.

anchors.title: Proposal: Regional bus rapid transit network for Texas Triangle
anchors.body:
I propose the state of Texas invest in a regional Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) network connecting the four major cities of the Texas Triangle: Austin, San Antonio, Houston, and Dallas-Fort Worth. BRT offers 80% of the capacity of light rail at 20% of the cost, with dedicated lanes, level boarding, and frequent service.

This intercity BRT network would reduce highway congestion, provide affordable travel options, and create an economic corridor connecting 75% of the state's population.
